answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This exact sentence is spoken by the narrator Victor Frankenstein in the closing volume of Mary Shelley’s novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818), confirmed word-for-word in the original 1818 text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Volume III, Chapter VI — narrated by Victor Frankenstein

source.excerpt: The rain had ceased for a moment, and I saw the fish play in the waters as they had done a few hours before; they had then been observed by Elizabeth. Nothing is so painful to the human mind as a great and sudden change. The sun might shine, or the clouds might lour; but nothing could appear to me as it had done the day before. A fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness: no creature had ever been so miserable as I was; so frightful an event is single in the history of man.
trail: First published anonymously in three volumes in 1818; the exact sentence appears near the novel's end, confirmed against a transcription of the original text on Wikisource ↗.
The identical wording also appears in a full-text scan of the 1818 first edition hosted by the Internet Archive ↗, independently corroborating the Wikisource transcription.
source.excerptNote: Spoken by narrator Victor Frankenstein while rowing back to Geneva, hours after discovering that his bride Elizabeth has been murdered on their wedding night.

author.name: Mary Shelley
author.heading: About Mary Shelley
author.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley wrote Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus at just eighteen, publishing it anonymously in 1818; it became one of the founding works of science fiction. She was the daughter of philosophers William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, and married the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley.

context.heading: Where it falls in the story
lead: The line arrives in the novel’s final act. Victor Frankenstein’s bride, Elizabeth, has just been murdered by his creature on their wedding night, and Victor is rowing back across Lake Geneva in shock. He notices fish playing in the water exactly as they had a few hours earlier, when Elizabeth was still alive — and the ordinary, unchanged world becomes unbearable against the enormity of what has just happened to him.

That contrast — a world that looks identical while everything inside a person has been shattered — is what the line is describing, and it is likely why the sentence has traveled so far outside the Gothic novel that contains it, still quoted today in writing about grief, trauma, and sudden loss.
